# Supplier-Caused Escape to Alternate Source

Chain 5. `ncr-writeup` → `root-cause-capa` → `supplier-quote-request`.

**The plugin's cross-area proof point.** A quality finding automatically
starting a sourcing action essentially never happens today, because quality and
purchasing live in different systems and different departments. That handoff is
the whole point of this chain.

If a part has exactly one qualified supplier and that supplier has a quality
problem, production stops. Sourcing an alternate is insurance, and the value is
in starting early: qualifying one takes weeks to months and nothing here
shortens that.

**Quick start**

```
→ A nonconformance traced to purchased material starts it
→ Root cause established against the SUPPLIER, not the process
→ Gate 1: a supplier-caused determination is a commercial claim. It needs an owner
→ Corrective action recorded
→ Build the alternate-source RFQ. Response format forces comparable bids
→ Gate 2: nothing outbound without release
→ THREE timestamps, not two. The middle one cannot be reconstructed later
```

---

## Inputs

| Input | Source | Form |
|---|---|---|
| The nonconformance | Inspector notes, an inspection export, a customer complaint | Conversation, M365, pasted |
| Drawing and specification | M365 document library | PDF |
| Everything else | Whatever the three member skills read | See each skill |

---

## The four steps

**1. A nonconformance traced to purchased material starts it.** `ncr-writeup`
writes it against its requirement, scopes the suspect quantity, and places every
part across the five containment locations. Where containment finds parts at or
past a customer, the escape notification drafts automatically against its
contractual clock.

**2. Root cause is established against the supplier rather than the process**,
through `root-cause-capa`. Lot clustering is the signal that points here: do
the failures group by material lot rather than by shift, operator or machine?

**Gate 1** — a supplier-caused determination is a commercially significant
claim. It says a named vendor caused a defect and it starts a search for an
alternate source. It needs a human owner.

**3. Corrective action is recorded** — the 8D, with D7 addressing the
system-level change.

**4. Build the RFQ package for an alternate source** through
`supplier-quote-request`: the drawing and specification at the verified current
revision, the demand picture, the quality clauses, the commercial terms, and a
**response schedule that forces comparable bids**.

**Gate 2** — nothing goes outbound until a person releases it.

**The chain ends at release; the sourcing event does not.** After it,
`supplier-quote-request` carries the event on: one email draft per supplier
for the buyer to send, response tracking and chases, the returned bids read
into one shape and compared, and a recommendation. The buyer decides, and the
skill records who and when. Nothing there is a third gate of this chain.

---

## Approval gates

| Gate | Where | What it protects |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | After step 2 | The supplier-caused determination has a named human owner before it acts |
| 2 | Before step 4 sends | Nothing reaches a supplier unreleased |

The flag carries its own `approval_state`, and `supplier-quote-request`
**checks the gate** rather than assuming the flag's existence implies it. An
unapproved flag is reported as a finding that needs an owner, not acted on.

---

## Three timestamps, not two

The chain's headline metric is **time from escape to alternate-source RFQ
issued**, and it cannot be owned by one skill: root cause analysis sits in the
middle of that window and can take days or weeks. So it is measured in two
segments, which needs three stamps.

| Stamp | Written by | On |
|---|---|---|
| `escape_detected_at` | `ncr-writeup`, when containment first places parts at or past a customer | `ncr.md` |
| `determination_made_at` | `root-cause-capa`, when the flag is raised | `supplier-caused-flag.md` |
| `rfq_issued_at` | `supplier-quote-request`, when the package goes out | Its own sourcing record |

**The middle one is the one that gets dropped, and the only one that cannot be
reconstructed afterwards.** The chain's output says so beside the stamp, every
run: *"determination_made_at — the middle of the three; this cannot be
reconstructed afterwards."* A stamp with no such line is the one a later
reader assumes could be backfilled. Without it the two segments collapse into a single
number, and the second segment — the dead time this chain actually eliminates —
disappears behind an investigation that legitimately takes weeks.

Keeping it segmented is what makes the improvement legible. Cutting the handoff
from two weeks to two days shows up even while the investigation still takes a
week. One blended figure would hide which half moved.

# Time alignment — the highest-risk failure mode in the skill

Getting the timeline right is most of the work in a root cause investigation,
and getting it wrong produces a **spurious correlation stated confidently**,
which is worse than producing nothing.

This is the highest-risk correctness issue in the whole plugin, alongside

## Why it goes wrong

Four systems recording the same event will disagree about when it happened:

| Source | How it usually records time |
|---|---|

# The two hard stops

Most of this skill assembles a package and reports what is missing. Two
conditions are different: they **block**, and no amount of user insistence
converts them into a warning.

---

## 1. Revision mismatch

**The revision in the document library must match the revision on the ERP item
master. When they disagree, stop.**

This is not a data-quality nicety. **Sending a supplier the wrong revision is
the classic and expensive error this skill exists to prevent**, and it is
expensive in a specific way: nothing goes wrong for months. The supplier quotes
the drawing you sent, wins the business, tools up, and ships parts that are
correct against the print in their hand and wrong against the one in yours. You
find out at first article if you are lucky, and at the customer if you are not.

### What to check

| Check | Where |
|---|---|
| Revision on the drawing file itself | The title block, not the filename. Filenames lie |
| Revision recorded in the document library | M365 metadata or the library's own record |
| Revision on the ERP item master | Where the profile's `### ERP scope` says revision lives: a named field, the item-ID suffix with its pattern, or not in the ERP. **Never inferred**: with no setting, say the ERP's revision location is not set and that the check could not use the ERP |
| Revision the current demand was ordered against | Open purchase orders and sales orders |

**Read the title block, not the filename.** `4471-B-RevC-final-v2.pdf` tells you
what somebody typed. The title block tells you what the drawing is.

### What to report

Name both revisions, both sources, and both dates. Do not resolve it — this is
a controlled-document question with an owner, and that owner is not the skill.

> *"Stopping before assembling the package. The document library holds
> 4471-B at Rev C, dated 2026-06-11. The NetSuite item master records Rev B, and
> the open demand on PO-8841 was placed against Rev B. Those cannot both be
> current. Either the item master was not updated when C released, or C was
> released and never flowed to purchasing.*
>
> *That distinction matters to the quote, because the two revisions differ. I
> need document control to confirm which revision this sourcing action is
> against before anything goes to a supplier."*

### The one thing not to do

Do not send both revisions and let the supplier work it out. It looks helpful. It
produces bids that are not comparable, and it tells the supplier that your
configuration control is unreliable, which is a bad thing for them to know while
they are pricing you.

---

## 2. Restricted data

**ITAR, EAR, export-controlled, or otherwise restricted technical data must not
be assembled into an outbound package without an explicit gate.** This is
blocking, and it blocks before assembly rather than before sending.

The reason for the ordering: once restricted geometry is collated into a package
that is one click from an email, the control has already been weakened. Stop at
the point of gathering.

### How it shows up

- An ITAR or EAR marking in the drawing title block or border
- A distribution statement, or "export controlled" in a document header
- A customer program known to be defence, space or controlled — captured in

- A supplier who is not on the plant's cleared list for that program

### What to do

Report it as blocking, name what was found and where, and state the specific
question that needs answering — usually whether the candidate supplier holds the
required registration and whether an export authorization covers the disclosure.

**Do not assess eligibility.** Whether a given supplier may receive controlled
technical data is a compliance determination with a named owner at the plant. The
skill's job is to notice, stop, and route it there.

---

## Why these two and not the rest

Everything else this skill finds goes on the missing-items list and the user
decides. These two are different because **both produce a harm that lands
somewhere other than where the mistake was made** — with a supplier who built to
the wrong print, or with a compliance exposure the plant carries.

A missing lead-time requirement produces a worse bid, and that is visible
immediately. These two are not visible until much later, which is exactly why
they are gates rather than warnings.

…

=== SUPPLIER RFQ PACKAGE — SENDABLE ===
…
=== END ===

## What a command-center page actually is

**Two kinds, and a skill always knows which one it produced.**

**A live dashboard**, for Operations and Quality. Published to the user's
Claude artifact store on the first run and updated in place at the same URL on
every later run, per `live-dashboard.md`. The artifact store is the user's own
Claude account, not M365 and not a system of record, so publishing to it does
not break the rule above.

**An offered page**, for Sales and Supply Chain, and for Operations or Quality
whenever the dashboard could not be published this run. An artifact produced
in the conversation that the user places: a page they open, read, and save or
forward, written as **a replacement for the last one**, carrying the same
sections in the same order, so a person can put it where the previous version
lived and read the delta at a glance. The plugin does not put it there.

**"Updated" is allowed only after a successful publish.** A skill may say it
updated a dashboard only when the publish call returned a URL in this same
run. Everywhere else the page was *offered*, and the skill says so. Reporting a
panel as updated when a page was offered is the false statement this file was
written to stop, and it still is.

no skill says it is shared.
